RagShortTexts: A long haft extends reach but needs clearance for swing and recovery in woods or doorways.
Secure heads and sound hafts matter; military repairs compete with timber and cart work.

Variants.Content: Axes in Rus and neighboring wooded lands serve timber work and close fighting, with use shaped by haft length, head weight and skill. A longer haft extends reach but catches around branches, shields and doors. Recovery after a blow matters alongside impact. Edges, sockets and wood need inspection after damp camps and long journeys.

An axeman needs room among companions and attention to footing and branches in woodland. A missed blow or an edge caught in timber leaves an opening. Marching halts allow checks for loose heads and splitting hafts. Cooperation with a shield bearer includes making movements clear so friendly men need not dodge the weapon.

A lord distinguishes timber work, barrier clearing and close combat when allocating axes and men. Skilled carpenters are valuable at bridges and forts and may be poorly spent in a front rank. Committing every good axe to an assault hampers camp timber work. Spare hafts, edge repairs and room on wooded roads remain necessary.

Household axes provide firewood, roofing and fences; requisition delays even winter fuel gathering. Borrowers need to account for broken hafts and damaged edges. Carpenter and smith perform different repairs. Giving military axes priority can leave a cultivator waiting another day for an essential tool.
